analysis.title: Synthetic study
analysis.summary: A made-up study that shows how fvTrace works. Its proofs are placeholders, so its verdicts are an illustration, not evidence.

questions.title: Effect
questions.text: Does the treatment change the marker?

facts.subject: S
facts.text: The analysis subtracts the control group's average marker level from the treated group's average.

evidence.summary: A placeholder Lean proof that stands in for the calculation.

facts.why: The claim uses this difference, so the calculation must match it.

facts.subject: S
facts.text: Treated samples have a higher average marker level, and chance alone rarely gives a difference this large.
facts.why: The claim says chance rarely gives this difference, so the data must show it.

facts.subject: S
facts.text: Rerunning the randomization gives the recorded groups.
facts.why: Otherwise the samples may not have been split the way the records say.

facts.subject: S
facts.text: The samples were split into the two groups at random, before anything was known about their marker levels.
facts.why: Otherwise another difference between the groups could explain the result.

facts.subject: S
facts.text: The samples are independent: treating one sample does not change another sample's marker level.
facts.why: Otherwise the treated samples could change the control samples, and the comparison would be wrong.

facts.subject: S
facts.text: When samples are split at random and do not affect each other, the group difference matches the average effect of the treatment, on average across all possible splits.

evidence.summary: A placeholder Lean proof that stands in for the randomization result.

facts.why: It is the reason the difference can be read as the effect of the treatment.

facts.subject: S
facts.text: If the treatment did nothing, checking every possible split of the samples shows how often chance alone gives a difference this large.
facts.why: It is the reason the data can say how rarely chance gives this difference.

facts.subject: N
facts.text: In the new cohort's table, the treated group's average marker level is higher.
facts.why: The claim says the treated average is higher, so the new data must show that.

claims.question: Q1
claims.subject: S
claims.text: On average over all fair random assignments, the difference between treated and control samples equals the treatment's average effect on these samples.
claims.headline: The difference between treated and control samples measures the average effect of the treatment.

claims.question: Q1
claims.subject: S
claims.text: If the treatment did nothing, a difference this large would arise by chance in fewer than 1 in 20 random assignments.
claims.headline: Treated samples show a rise that chance alone rarely produces.

claims.question: Q1
claims.subject: N
claims.text: In the new cohort's data table, the treated samples' average marker level is higher than the controls'.
claims.headline: In the new cohort, treated samples show a higher average marker level.

experiments.subject: S
experiments.title: Check the result
experiments.method: Finish the proof that counting every possible split gives the chance of this difference, then run its proved checker on the result table.
experiments.resources: Result table and the records of the groups.
experiments.caveat: Inconclusive when the table is incomplete or the proof is not finished.

experiments.subject: N
experiments.title: Collect a new cohort
experiments.method: Sample new animals and run the proved checker on their data.

experiments.subject: S
experiments.title: Rerun the randomization
experiments.method: A proved checker reruns the randomization program with its recorded settings and compares its groups with the records.
experiments.resources: The randomization program, its settings and the records.
experiments.caveat: Shows that the records match the program, not that the samples were handled as recorded.

waivers.reason: The test counts every possible split of the samples, so it needs no statistical model.
